title: Dream for Winter
text:
In winter we will go away, on blue cushions,

in a little pink carriage.

So comfortable, while a nest of mad kisses sleeps

in every soft corner.


You will close your eyes so as not to look through the windows

at night and its black grimaces,

threatening monsters, black wolves, black devils

like an atrocious crowd.


Then you will feel a scratch on your cheek...

And a kiss will run over you, like a crazed spider,

crazed along your neck.


And you will say to me: "Look, look!" inclining your head.

—But how long it will take us to find that creature

that travels and travels without aim...!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the playful winter carriage fantasy and the spider-like wandering kiss.

title: Head of a Faun
text:
In the foliage, green case that gold gilds,

in the foliage, uncertain and clotted with flowers

that bloom magnificent, where a kiss dwells,

nervous, while tearing the splendid embroideries,


a frightened faun arches his brow,

biting the red flowers with his white teeth.

Dark, stained with blood, like aged wine,

his lip bursts into laughter, lost among leaves.


And when, like a squirrel, through the fronds he is startled,

caught on the branches his laughter shivers;

and we see, frightened by the singing chaffinch,

how the golden Kiss of the Forest falls asleep.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the faun's leafy emergence and the forest kiss falling asleep.

title: The Cupboard
text:
A great carved cupboard—the dark oak

emanates the goodness of the old, so old;

it is open, and its depths pour, like aged wine,

dark waves of obsessive aromas.


Stuffed full, it is a jumble of old antiquities,

perfumed yellow sheets, little rags

of women and children, wrinkled laces,

grandmother's shawls with painted dragons.


In it we would find medallions and locks

of white or blond hair, portraits, dried flowers

whose smell mixes with the smell of fruit.


Oh, old cupboard, how many stories you know!

And you would like to tell them; that is why, uncertain, you creak

when your black doors slowly open.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the cupboard as an archive of scents, keepsakes, and creaking stories.

title: The Wench
text:
In the brown dining room, perfumed by a

mixture of fruit smell and varnish, at ease,

I got myself a plate of some Belgian stew

or other, and settled into an enormous chair.


While I ate, I heard the clock—happy, quiet...

The kitchen opened, an immense gust,

—and the maid entered; and I do not quite know why

she wore her shawl open and a mischievous hairstyle.


And while she ran her startled finger

over her face, velvet, white and pink peach,

making a naive gesture with her little-girl lip,


she set the plates beside me, calming me.

And then, distracted, to earn a kiss,

softly: "touch, touch: my face

has gotten cold..."
editorial_note: The translation keeps the tavern intimacy, Belgian stew, and playful request for a kiss.

title: Dark and Puckered Like a Purple Carnation...
text:
Dark and puckered like a purple carnation,

it breathes, humbly sheltered among moss,

still moist from the love that slowly flows

down her white buttocks to its fringed edge.


Filaments like milk tears

wept, rejected by the monstrous squall,

crossing little clots of pink mud

toward where the slope calls them to lose themselves.


My dream has often joined itself to its suction cup;

my soul, longing for material coitus,

made it its tear duct and dwelling of its weepings.


It is the fainting olive tree, and the mimosa flute;

it is the tube where glorious sweets descend:

feminine Canaan isolated among dampness!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the deliberately grotesque erotic blazon and its floral-biblical exaggeration.

title: Venus Anadyomene
text:
Like from a green tin coffin,

with slicked-down dark hair, and deficiencies

very badly concealed, from an ancient bathtub

a woman's face emerges, slow and crude.


The neck follows next, fat and gray, and bony

shoulders, a back that hesitates in its coming out,

and then the loins want to take flight:

under the skin, suet, in layers, like puff pastry.


The spine, red, and the whole present

a dreadful aftertaste, and above all one observes

details that must be analyzed with a magnifying glass.


The back bears two words: CLARA VENUS.

A body that writhes and offers its saddle

beautiful, with its ulcer, dark, in the anus.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Rimbaud's anti-Venus grotesque and its clinical final detail.

title: The Punishment of Tartuffe
text:
Fanning, like fire, a loving heart

under chaste black cloak, happy, gloved hand,

one day as he went, atrocious, meek, yellow,

drooling his faith through his toothless mouth,


one day as he went, "Oremus," a Devil

grabbed him roughly by his pious ear,

letting loose frightful words at him, and tearing

the chaste black cloak from his warm sweaty skin.


Punishment!... His clothes are unbuttoned,

and his long rosary of remiss sins

parade over his chest; Saint Tartuffe is pale!...


He was confessing, at last, praying amid death rattles!

And the man could only carry off his ruffles...

—Tartuffe is completely naked, ugh, how disgusting!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the anticlerical undressing farce and Tartuffe's exposed hypocrisy.

title: The Sleeper of the Valley
text:
A hole of green, where a river sings,

hooking, crazily, through the grass, shreds

of silver; where the sun from the proud mountain

shines: a hollow growing in moss and light.


A soldier, bareheaded and open-mouthed,

his nape bathed by cool blue watercress,

sleeps, stretched out beneath the clouds, in the grass,

pale, in his bed on which the sun rains.


With his feet among gladioli he sleeps and smiles as

a sick child smiles; surely he is dreaming:

Nature, cradle him warmly: he is cold.


His nostril no longer quivers with the field's scent;

he sleeps in the sun; his hand on his calm breast;

with two red holes in his right side.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the pastoral lullaby structure and the final revelation of the wounds.

title: My Bohemia
text:
(Fantasy)


I went off, fists in my torn pockets...

my waistcoat too was becoming ideal,

walking beneath the open sky, Muse, I was so faithful to you!

how many great loves, ah ah ah, I dreamed myself!


My only pair of trousers was a huge tear.

—Dreaming Tom Thumb, I scattered on my way

rhymes. And my inn was the Great Bear.

—My stars trembled with a sweet rustle.


And I listened to them, at the roadside

when September evenings fall, feeling

dew on my forehead, like a wine of life.


And rhyming, lost, through fantastic shadows,

I stretched the laces, as if they were lyres,

of my torn shoes, beside my heart.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the vagabond poet's torn pockets, star-inn, and shoes turned into lyres.

title: Rages of Caesars
text:
The bloodless Man, through flowering meadows,

walks, dressed in black, cigar in mouth;

the bloodless Man evokes Tuileries in bloom,

—and his dead eye sometimes takes on gleams of fire...


Drunk, the Emperor, after twenty years of orgy,

thought: "I will blow on Liberty

very carefully, as on a candle!"

Liberty is reborn!... —and he is broken-backed!


He is imprisoned. —What name on his echoless lips

throbs? what implacable longing bites him?

No one will know, for Caesar has the dead eye.


Perhaps he thinks of his little-bespectacled Crony...

—And look how from his lit cigar flows,

as in Saint-Cloud, at night, the tenuous blue cloud.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the satirical imperial portrait, dead eye, and cigar-smoke memory.
